newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices slip as heating oil crunch eases.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices slip as heating oil crunch eases.

text.p: Oil prices shed more than $1.0 a barrel in frantic business just before the close of business in London as a combination of resumed Iraqi crude oil exports and the end of a big heating oil shortfall punched a hole in the market.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea for January delivery sank to a new low of $22.00 a barrel, a fall of $1.29 a barrel and the lowest seen since November. Brokers said funds were heavy sellers.
Brent recovered slightly to close $1.13 a barrel down at $22.16 a barrel.

The contract opened the day weak after closing 81 cents lower on Tuesday, when Iraq was due to start its first oil exports in six years although the actual flow was held up and began in earnest on Wednesday.
"It was the realisation that Iraqi crude is going to hit and the delayed reaction to that. The funds took hold of it and decided that oil was not a market to be in," said a futures broker.
After the market closed on Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute (API) said stocks of U.S. crude oil, distillates -- mostly heating oil -- and gasoline rose last week.

The rise was largely the result of higher refinery output and a 1.5 million barrel per day (bpd) jump in imports. U.S. heating oil stocks in the key Northeast region remained 29 percent below last year's levels but better than the 40 percent deficit earlier this year.

Stock building, mild weather forecasts for the U.S. northeast, the world's largest heating oil consumer, and the resumption of Iraqi oil flows after a six-year absence, took $2.00 off the oil price since last week.

"Sentiment in the complex has clearly become more negative with the (mild) weather not helping...there are a number of bearish fundamental influences weighing" in, said brokers GNI in their daily report.
But some traders said it was too early into the winter to sell the market short since heating oil inventories on both sides of the Atlantic are still down from 1995 levels.

"Technically, it is under pressure right now but it can easily bounce back. The winter is just beginning and the underlying tone is bullish," said Oystein Berentsen, head of international crude oil trading at Norwegian state oil company Statoil.

Berentsen said the market could easily absorb the 500,000 to 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude exports which should hit the market soon now that the much-delayed U.N. "food-for-oil" plan has been approved.
"Iraqi oil could not have hit the market at a better time. The demand is there," Berentsen said.
On Tuesday, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein ceremoniously hit the switch which should have sent 650,000 bpd of Iraqi crude through a pipeline to Turkey's Ceyhan port on the Mediterranean.

A technical glitch meant that no oil actually made it to Turkey, although the state-run Turkish Anatolian news agency said the oil flow began around 1000 GMT on Wednesday at a rate of 350,000 barrels per day.
The absence of Iraqi crude from tight oil markets was partly the reason why prices shot to a near six-year high in October.
Crude oil prices remain on average around $3.0 a barrel higher than this time last year.
Under the U.N. deal signed in May, Iraq is allowed to sell $2.0 billion worth of crude oil for six months to buy food and medicines under strict U.N. supervision.
Iraq said it would pump 650,000 bpd of crude oil through its pipeline to Ceyhan and through its Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr under the U.N. plan cleared on Monday.

Turkey has signed up for Iraqi crude and interest from other oil companies picked up on Wednesday. U.S. oil company Coastal Corp said it was waiting for U.S. Treasury approval of a contract signed with Iraqi state oil marketing organisation SOMO.
Brazil's state oil company Petrobras said it was negotiating a price formula with Iraq to lift 20,000-30,000 bpd of crude. France's Elf and Total are said to be close to signing contracts also.

Iraq, before the Gulf War the second biggest oil producer in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) after Saudi Arabia, produced 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude in July 1990.
